pages.h1: Chest pain: a focused urgent history
pages.meta_description: Hear and read a complete, patient-friendly English history for acute chest pain, from immediate safety checks to a concise closing summary.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Johnson, 58, has had central chest pain for two hours.

voice.direction: A focused emergency consultation in clear American English. The doctor is mature, calm, concise, and reassuring without sounding casual. The patient is a 58-year-old man in significant discomfort: worried, slightly breathless, and natural, but always intelligible. Keep pauses brief because the history is urgent.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The pain is central and radiates to the left arm. What should you ask next to characterize it?
The patient is clammy and short of breath. Which immediately relevant discriminator or danger feature should you ask about next?

recall.cue: Ask one focused question that would refine this patient’s cardiovascular risk.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Lee. I can see you're in pain. We're going to assess you right away. While the nurse connects the monitor and gets an ECG, tell me what happened.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I've had this pain in the middle of my chest for about two hours. I thought it was heartburn, but it isn't going away.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What were you doing when it started?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I was sitting at the kitchen table. It came on while I was resting.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Can you point to where you feel it? Does it spread anywhere else?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's right behind my breastbone, and it goes down my left arm.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How would you describe it in your own words?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's a heavy pressure, almost like something is sitting on my chest.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: On a scale from zero to ten, how strong is it now? Has it been there continuously?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About seven out of ten. Yes, it has been constant.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you felt short of breath, sweaty, nauseated, or lightheaded with it?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I've been clammy and a little short of breath. I haven't vomited or passed out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does taking a deep breath, moving, or pressing on your chest change the pain?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Nothing seems to change it. I tried antacids, but they did nothing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did the pain tear through to your back, or did you suddenly feel faint when it began?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had anything similar before, even if it went away?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Actually, twice in the past two weeks I felt a milder pressure walking uphill. It stopped when I rested, so I ignored it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I have high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. I'm not sure about my cholesterol.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke? And has anyone in your close family had heart disease?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I smoke about a pack a day and have for twenty years. My father died of a heart attack at sixty-two.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What medicines do you take, and have you ever had a serious reaction to aspirin or any other medicine?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Metformin and lisinopril. I don't have any medicine allergies that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What is worrying you most right now?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I'm scared this is a heart attack, like my dad had.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I understand. You have had two hours of constant central pressure at rest, spreading to your left arm, with sweating and shortness of breath. You also had two recent episodes with exertion and have several heart risk factors. Have I understood that correctly?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes, that's right.

flow: Stabilize while talking
Pin down onset
Map pain and associated symptoms
Check immediate alternatives
Find prior episodes and risk factors
Summarize without delaying care
do_not_miss: Pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes
Spread to an arm, jaw, back, or shoulder
Shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or fainting
Previous exertional episodes
Cardiovascular history, smoking, diabetes, and family history

sources.title: American Heart Association — Acute Coronary Syndrome

pages.h1: Abdominal cramps and loose stools: a model history
pages.meta_description: Hear and read a complete English history for recurrent abdominal cramps and loose stools, including bowel pattern, red flags, triggers, and patient concerns.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Davies, 31, has had abdominal cramps and loose stools for over a year.

voice.direction: A relaxed outpatient consultation in natural American English. The doctor has a clear, attentive voice and uses short reflective pauses. The patient is a friendly 31-year-old man who is mildly embarrassed about bowel symptoms and becomes more open as the conversation continues.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The bowel pattern and pain-relief link are established. What associated symptom or alarm feature should you ask about next?
Important alarm features are negative. Which exposure, medicine, food, or stress trigger should you explore next?

recall.cue: Acknowledge the concern, then ask one question about function or the patient’s goal.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Davies, I'm Dr. Patel. What would you like us to focus on today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: For more than a year I've had stomach cramps and loose bowel movements. It's getting difficult to manage at work.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Tell me what a typical episode is like, from the beginning.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I get cramping low down in my abdomen, then I suddenly need the bathroom. The stool is usually loose and watery.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How often does that happen, and how long has this pattern been going on?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Three or four days most weeks. It started about fourteen months ago.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What happens to the cramping after you have a bowel movement?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It usually eases within about half an hour.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Besides the cramping and loose stool, do you get bloating, nausea, or vomiting?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I get very bloated by late afternoon. No nausea or vomiting.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do the symptoms ever wake you at night? Have you noticed blood in the stool?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No to both. Once I'm asleep, they don't wake me, and I've never seen blood.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had a fever, lost weight without trying, or felt unusually tired or weak?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No fever or weight loss. I work long hours, so I'm tired sometimes, but not in a new way.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any greasy stool, very pale stool, or trouble flushing it away?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. It's loose, but I haven't noticed anything like that.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you noticed any foods, drinks, medicines, travel, or stressful situations that change the symptoms?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Deadlines definitely make it worse. I also drink about four cups of coffee a day. I haven't traveled recently or taken antibiotics.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you tried changing what you eat or taking anything for it?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I skip breakfast before meetings and sometimes take an over-the-counter diarrhea medicine. It helps a little.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other medical conditions, and what regular medicines or supplements do you take?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I have anxiety and take sertraline, fifty milligrams a day. That's all.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any medicine allergies? And do you smoke, vape, or drink alcohol?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No known allergies. I vape socially and drink a couple of beers on weekends.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does anyone in your family have inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, or bowel cancer?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: An older cousin has Crohn's disease. That's what has me worried.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How is this affecting you day to day, and what were you hoping we could help with?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I'm afraid of getting urgent diarrhea in front of clients. I want to know it isn't Crohn's and find a way to control it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me check that I have the story right. For fourteen months you have had lower abdominal cramps and loose stools on three or four days a week. The pain improves after a bowel movement, and stress and coffee seem to worsen it. You have bloating, but no nighttime diarrhea, bleeding, fever, or unplanned weight loss. Your main concern is Crohn's disease and the effect on client meetings. Is there anything important I missed?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, that's exactly it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Thank you. We'll examine you and decide which focused tests are appropriate before we talk through the possible causes and options together.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That sounds good.

flow: Let the patient describe the pattern
Connect pain with bowel movements
Characterize stool and associated symptoms
Screen for alarm features
Explore triggers and self-treatment
Ask about family history and impact
Summarize and verify
do_not_miss: Blood in the stool
Symptoms waking the patient at night
Unplanned weight loss, fever, or anemia symptoms
Family history of inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer
Recent travel, antibiotics, and medication triggers

sources.title: American College of Gastroenterology — IBS Clinical Guideline summary

pages.h1: Low mood and loss of interest: a model mental health history
pages.meta_description: Hear and read an empathetic English mental health history that explores depressive symptoms and moves directly, safely, and calmly into suicide risk assessment.
pages.patient_card: Mrs. Clark, 45, has felt persistently low and unlike herself for three months.

voice.direction: A private mental health consultation in gentle, unhurried American English. The doctor sounds warm, grounded, and direct when discussing safety. The patient is a 45-year-old woman with low energy and long response latencies; she sounds sad and tired but remains clear. Do not make the performance melodramatic.

prediction_pauses.prompt: Low mood, loss of interest, and early waking are present. Which symptom domain should you assess next?
Psychosis and mania screens are negative. What coping behavior and then safety question must follow?
The patient reports a passive death wish but no current intent or plan. Which part of risk and protective assessment comes next?

recall.cue: Use calm, direct language to ask the most important immediate safety follow-up.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mrs. Clark, I'm Dr. Rivera. We have privacy here, and we can take this at your pace. What has been happening?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: For about three months I've felt very low. Everything feels heavy, and I don't feel like myself anymore.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What does a difficult day look like for you?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I force myself to go to work at the library, but I move slowly and can't concentrate. At home I just sit on the couch.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What has happened to the things you usually enjoy?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I stopped playing the piano and reading. I used to love both, but now I feel nothing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How has your sleep been?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I fall asleep, but I wake around three every morning and can't get back to sleep.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How are your appetite, energy, and concentration?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I eat because I know I should. I have almost no energy, and I keep losing my place at work.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you been blaming yourself or feeling that you are letting people down?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: All the time. I feel like a failure as a mother and an employee, even over small mistakes from years ago.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever heard or seen things other people couldn't, or felt that someone was trying to harm you?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energized or confident, needed very little sleep, talked much more than usual, or acted impulsively?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, I've never had anything like that.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you been drinking more alcohol or using any drugs or medicines to cope?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No drugs. I might have one glass of wine on the weekend, but not more than before.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You said everything feels heavy. In the past few weeks, have you wished you were dead or wished you could go to sleep and not wake up?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes. Sometimes I wish I just wouldn't wake up.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. Are you having thoughts of killing yourself right now?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I don't want to kill myself. I just want this pain to stop.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you thought about how you might kill yourself, made a plan, or taken any steps toward one?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I haven't made a plan or done anything.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have access to a gun or a large supply of medicines at home?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: There are no guns. We have normal household medicines, nothing I've been collecting.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever tried to kill yourself or deliberately hurt yourself in the past?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, never.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What has helped you stay safe when those thoughts appear? Who could you contact today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I think about my daughter. My sister knows I've been struggling, and she would come if I called.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you feel able to stay safe today, and would you tell your sister or contact urgent help if the thoughts became active or you started making a plan?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes. I can call my sister, and I can tell someone if it gets worse.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You had one similar episode eight years ago. What treatment did you receive then?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I took sertraline and saw a therapist. Both helped, and I eventually felt like myself again.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What are you hoping we can help you with now?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I want to sleep and feel some joy again. I'm frightened that I'll always feel this way.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me summarize. For three months you have had persistent low mood, loss of interest, early waking, low energy, poor concentration, and strong guilt that are affecting work and home. You sometimes wish you would not wake up, but you deny current suicidal thoughts, a plan, or past attempts. Your daughter and sister are important supports, and treatment helped before. Is that accurate?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Our first priority is your safety. Before you leave, we will complete a fuller safety assessment and make a written plan with your sister's contact and crisis support. Then we can discuss treatment and close follow-up together.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay. I'm relieved I told you.

flow: Create privacy and pace
Explore mood, pleasure, and function
Ask about biological and cognitive symptoms
Screen for mania, psychosis, and substances
Ask directly about suicide
Assess plan, means, history, and supports
Close with a concrete safety process
do_not_miss: Current suicidal thoughts
Plan, method, access to means, and intent
Past attempts or self-harm
Manic or psychotic symptoms
Protective factors, support, and ability to stay safe

sources.title: NIMH — Adult Outpatient Brief Suicide Safety Assessment Guide

pages.h1: Painful periods and pelvic pain: a model gynecology history
pages.meta_description: Hear and read a respectful English gynecology history covering painful periods, deep pain during sex, bowel symptoms, and fertility goals without assumptions.
pages.patient_card: Ms. Yoon, 32, has worsening period pain and has been trying to conceive for one year.

voice.direction: A respectful gynecology consultation in warm, clear American English. The doctor is calm and matter-of-fact about sensitive questions. The patient is a 32-year-old woman who sounds thoughtful and increasingly worried when discussing fertility. Avoid euphemistic or melodramatic delivery.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The pain pattern, cycle, and last menstrual period are clear. What bleeding feature should you ask about next?
Deep pain during sex is present. Which infection risk or cyclical pelvic symptom should you explore next?
A year of regular unprotected intercourse and no prior testing are established. What pregnancy or sexual-history clarification belongs next?

recall.cue: Ask one background question that connects cyclical pelvic pain with the fertility history.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Ms. Yoon, I'm Dr. Morgan. What would you like help with today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My periods have become very painful, and my husband and I have been trying to get pregnant for a year without success.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Tell me how the pain has changed over that time.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It used to be manageable, but for the past year the cramps have become severe. I sometimes have to miss work.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Where do you feel the pain, and when does it begin in relation to your period?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Deep in my pelvis and lower back. It starts the day before my period and is worst for the first two days.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How long are your cycles, and when did your last period start?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: They're regular, about twenty-eight days. My last period started twelve days ago.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How long do you bleed, and has the amount changed?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About five days. It is a little heavier than it used to be, but I'm not soaking through a pad every hour.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have bleeding between periods or after sex?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I ask everyone with pelvic pain about sex because it can help us understand the pain. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes, that's okay.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have pain during sex? If so, does it feel near the entrance or deeper in the pelvis?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's a deep pain, especially with deeper penetration. That has also become worse this year.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any unusual vaginal discharge, fever, or history of a sexually transmitted infection or pelvic infection?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No discharge or fever, and I've never had an STI or pelvic infection.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do bowel movements or urination become painful around your period?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Bowel movements are more painful during my period. I have IBS, but this pain feels more tied to my cycle.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever been pregnant, had pelvic surgery, or been treated for any gynecologic condition?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No pregnancies and no surgery. I haven't had any gynecologic treatment.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Are you and your husband having sex regularly without birth control, and has either of you had fertility testing?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes, usually two or three times a week without birth control. Neither of us has had testing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Are there any other partners or pregnancy possibilities that would change which tests we should discuss?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, just my husband.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What medicines, supplements, or pain relievers do you use? Any medicine allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I take ibuprofen during my period and a prenatal vitamin. I don't have any known allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does anyone in your family have endometriosis or difficulty becoming pregnant?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My aunt had endometriosis. I don't know of fertility problems in anyone else.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What are you most concerned about, and what were you hoping would happen today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I'm worried the pain means I may never get pregnant. I've read about laparoscopy and want to know if I need it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me make sure I have this right. Over the past year your period pain has become severe enough to disrupt work. You also have deep pain during sex and bowel pain around your period. Your cycles are regular, and you have been having regular sex without birth control for a year without becoming pregnant. Your main concern is future fertility. Is that accurate?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes, exactly.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Thank you. We can now discuss an examination and a stepwise evaluation of both the pelvic pain and fertility. We will decide together which tests are useful and whether a procedure would add value.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

flow: Open with both concerns
Map pain to the menstrual cycle
Characterize bleeding
Ask permission before sexual history
Separate bowel and bladder patterns
Clarify pregnancy intention and fertility timeline
Summarize the patient's priority
do_not_miss: Last menstrual period and pregnancy possibility
Bleeding between periods or after sex
Pain during sex and whether it is superficial or deep
Cyclic bowel or bladder pain
Pelvic infection history
Pregnancy intention and duration of unprotected intercourse

sources.title: CDC — Guide to Taking a Sexual History

pages.h1: Constipation in a young child: a model parent history
pages.meta_description: Hear and read a complete English pediatric history for a three-year-old with painful, infrequent stools and stool-withholding behavior.
pages.patient_card: Sophia, 3, is brought in by her mother because bowel movements are hard and painful.

voice.direction: A calm pediatric visit in conversational American English. The doctor is friendly and clear, speaking first to the child and then to her mother without sounding patronizing. The parent is an attentive adult woman who is concerned and sometimes self-conscious about toilet training. The child does not have a separate speaking voice in this recording.

prediction_pauses.prompt: Painful hard stools and a small blood streak are present. Which complication or associated bowel pattern should you ask about next?
Growth and early meconium passage are reassuring. What onset or neurologic red flag still needs clarification?
Diet and attempted remedies are clear. Which behavior or environmental trigger should you explore next?

recall.cue: Ask one question that distinguishes a recent functional pattern from constipation beginning in infancy.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Hi, Sophia. I'm Dr. Chen. I'm going to talk with your mom about your tummy, and you can tell me anything you want. Mom, what has been happening?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: She only has a bowel movement about once every five days, and it is very hard and painful.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: When did this pattern begin?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: About four months ago, when we started toilet training. Before that she went more regularly.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What do the stools look like, and how does Sophia act when she needs to go?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: They are large, hard pieces. She crosses her legs, squeezes her bottom, and hides in a corner to hold it in.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does she cry with a bowel movement or have any blood on the stool or toilet paper?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: She cries because it hurts. I've seen a tiny streak of bright red blood twice, after a very hard stool.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does stool ever leak into her underwear between bowel movements?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: Sometimes there is a small smear, and I thought she wasn't wiping well.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does she have belly pain, swelling, vomiting, fever, or a poor appetite?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: Her belly aches before she goes, but it settles afterward. No vomiting or fever, and she eats normally.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Has she been growing as expected or losing weight?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: She has been growing normally and hasn't lost weight.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Thinking back to when she was born, did she pass her first dark stool within the first day or two?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: Yes, the hospital said everything was normal.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Has constipation been a problem since infancy, or is this the first period like this?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: This is the first time. She had normal soft stools as a baby.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any weakness in her legs, trouble walking, urine infections, or loss of bladder control?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: No. She runs everywhere and hasn't had urine infections.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What does she usually eat and drink in a day? How much milk does she have?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: She loves milk and probably drinks four cups. She is picky with vegetables, but she eats some fruit and drinks water.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you tried any stool softeners, suppositories, or other remedies?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: Only prune juice. I haven't given her medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How are you approaching toilet training right now?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: We ask her to sit after dinner, but she gets upset. Sometimes we push because we know she needs to go.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: This can become a painful cycle, and it is not her fault or yours. Has there been any major change at home or at daycare?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: She moved to a new daycare five months ago. She refuses to use their toilet.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does anyone in the family have severe constipation, thyroid disease, celiac disease, or Hirschsprung disease?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: No, nothing like that.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does Sophia take any regular medicine, vitamin, or iron? Does she have any medicine allergies?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: No regular medicines and no known allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me summarize. Sophia had normal stools from birth until toilet training began four months ago. She now passes a large, hard, painful stool about every five days and tries to hold it in. She sometimes has a small smear in her underwear and a streak of blood after a hard stool, but no persistent vomiting, swollen abdomen, poor growth, leg symptoms, or problems since birth. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: Yes, that's right.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Thank you. I'll examine her, including her growth and abdomen. Then we'll make a plan to soften the stools and take the pressure out of toilet time, with clear signs for when to contact us urgently.

turns.speaker: Parent
turns.text: That would be a relief.

flow: Speak to the child first
Ask the parent for the pattern
Describe stool and withholding behavior
Look for pain, soiling, and complications
Check onset from birth and growth
Explore diet, toilet training, and environment
Remove blame and summarize
do_not_miss: Delayed passage of meconium or symptoms from early infancy
Vomiting, marked abdominal distention, fever, weight loss, or poor growth
Blood not clearly limited to a hard-stool episode
Leg weakness, abnormal walking, or bladder symptoms
Stool withholding, fecal soiling, diet, and toilet-training stress

sources.title: ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN — Evaluation and Treatment of Functional Constipation

pages.h1: A severe one-sided headache: a model history
pages.meta_description: Read a structured English headache history covering onset, visual aura, associated symptoms, secondary-headache warning signs, medication use, and functional impact.
pages.patient_card: Ms. Yoon, 28, has had a severe right-sided throbbing headache for 24 hours after seeing flashing lights.

voice.direction: A quiet urgent neurology consultation in clear American English. The doctor is calm, precise, and considerate of light sensitivity. The patient is a 28-year-old woman speaking through significant headache and nausea but remaining natural and intelligible. Keep the pace measured without sounding sedated.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The visual symptoms spread gradually and then cleared. What comparison with earlier headaches should you make next?
The familiar aura and associated symptoms are established, with no focal deficit, fever, or stiff neck. Which secondary-headache context should you screen next?
Frequency, pattern change, acute-medicine use, and general health are clear. Which treatment-relevant background question belongs next?

recall.cue: Ask one question that checks acute-medicine use and possible medication overuse.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Ms. Yoon, I'm Dr. Rivera. I can see the light is bothering you, so we'll keep the room dim. Tell me what happened with this headache.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It started yesterday. I saw flashing lights, and about half an hour later I got a strong throbbing pain on the right side of my head.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How did the pain build up?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It became strong over maybe twenty minutes. It wasn't like a sudden explosion.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How severe is it now, and has it let up during the past twenty-four hours?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's about eight out of ten. It eased a little while I slept, but it never fully went away.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Describe exactly what you saw before the pain began.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: There were flickering, flashing spots across my vision. They gradually spread and then cleared after about twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Was that visual experience the same as with your earlier headaches?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yes. I've had the same warning before several of my headaches since I was a teenager.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What other symptoms came with this attack?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I feel nauseated, and I vomited twice. Light and ordinary sounds feel unbearable.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had any new weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, confusion, or loss of vision?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. The flashing stopped before the pain settled in, and I haven't had any of those other problems.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any fever or a stiff neck?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did this follow a head injury, heavy exertion, or a new medicine? Do you have cancer or a condition that weakens your immune system?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Nothing unusual happened before it started, and I don't have cancer or an immune condition.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How often are these headaches occurring now, and has their usual pattern changed?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Usually once or twice a month. This one feels like my usual attack, but it has lasted longer and has kept me from working.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What have you taken for it, and how often do you use pain medicine in a typical month?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I took ibuprofen yesterday, but it didn't help. I only use it on headache days, usually once or twice a month.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any other medical conditions or take any regular medicines?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I'm generally healthy and don't take anything regularly.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: None that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Because pregnancy can affect which causes and treatments we consider, is there any chance you could be pregnant?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, there isn't.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What are you most concerned about, and what help were you hoping for today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I'm worried these attacks will keep disrupting my design work. I'd like something that can stop them when they start.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me summarize. You developed your usual gradually spreading visual warning, followed thirty minutes later by a right-sided throbbing headache with vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound. The attack was not instantly severe, and you report no fever, stiff neck, injury, or new neurologic symptom. It resembles attacks you have had since adolescence, although it has lasted longer and ibuprofen did not help. Have I understood that correctly, and is there anything else I should know?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's correct. I don't think I've left anything out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I'll check your vital signs and perform a focused neurologic examination before we decide what evaluation and symptom relief are appropriate. If the pattern changes suddenly or you develop weakness, trouble speaking, confusion, fever, or a stiff neck, that needs urgent reassessment.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay. That makes sense.

flow: Reduce sensory discomfort and invite the story
Establish onset and time to peak
Characterize the visual symptoms and headache
Compare with prior attacks
Screen for secondary-headache warning signs
Review acute medication and relevant background
Explore work impact and treatment goal
Summarize and give a pattern-change safety net
do_not_miss: Sudden maximal onset or a new, worsening, or substantially changed pattern
Persistent visual loss, weakness, numbness, speech change, confusion, or reduced consciousness
Fever, stiff neck, recent head injury, pregnancy, cancer, or immune suppression
Frequency of attacks and acute-medication use
Functional impact and the patient's goal for rescue treatment

pages.h1: Wheezing during exercise: a model respiratory history
pages.meta_description: Read a patient-friendly English asthma history covering exercise and cold-air triggers, symptom control, severe-attack history, inhaler use, exposures, and patient goals.
pages.patient_card: Ms. Chloe Bennett, 32, develops wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath when she runs outdoors.

voice.direction: A routine respiratory clinic visit in conversational American English. The doctor is attentive and practical, with clear phrasing for inhaler technique and safety questions. The patient is a physically active 32-year-old woman who sounds well at rest but concerned about exercising alone.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The exercise trigger, timing, reliever response, and weekly frequency are clear. Which control domain should you assess next?
There are no nighttime or resting symptoms and no episode with speech difficulty or reliever failure. Which severe-attack history should you ask about next?
Past severity, inhaler technique, controller use, and exposures are established. Which atopic background or functional goal should come next?

recall.cue: After hearing how the reliever is used, ask one question about ongoing anti-inflammatory or controller treatment.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Ms. Bennett, I'm Dr. Lewis. What would you like us to focus on today?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I wheeze and get short of breath when I run, especially outside in cold weather. I'm worried it could turn into a serious asthma attack.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Tell me what you notice first during a run.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Usually a dry cough starts, then my chest feels tight and I hear a whistling sound when I breathe out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How soon does that begin, and what do you do when it happens?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It starts after about ten minutes in cold air. I stop, take my rescue inhaler, and the symptoms settle within ten or fifteen minutes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How many days a week are you needing the inhaler for these symptoms?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Usually two or three days a week, mostly on running days.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do coughing or breathing symptoms ever wake you at night?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I sleep through the night.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What is your breathing like at rest or during ordinary daily activities?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's normal. Walking and work don't bother me.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had a recent cold or noticed another trigger besides running and cold air?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No recent cold. I haven't found a clear trigger indoors.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had an attack where you could not speak in full sentences or the inhaler did not help?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I've always been able to speak, and the inhaler has worked.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever needed an emergency visit, hospital stay, or breathing tube because of asthma?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Nothing that severe.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Which inhaler do you use now? Please walk me through how you use it.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's an albuterol inhaler. I shake it, breathe out, press once while I breathe in, and then hold my breath. I don't use a spacer.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you use any controller inhaler or take any other regular medicine?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No controller and no other regular medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you smoke or vape, or breathe smoke or fumes at home or work?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I don't smoke or vape, my roommate doesn't smoke, and my office doesn't have fumes.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have eczema, nasal allergies, or a family history of asthma?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I had eczema as a child. I don't have nasal allergies, and no one else in my family has asthma.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No known medication allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How is this changing your exercise, and what would you like from today's visit?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I've stopped running alone because I'm scared I won't get help. I want to know how well controlled this is, whether I need a controller, and whether my technique is right.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You have cough, chest tightness, wheezing, and shortness of breath after about ten minutes of outdoor running, especially in cold air, on two or three days a week. Albuterol settles it within fifteen minutes. You have no nighttime or resting symptoms and no history of a severe attack, but fear of an attack is limiting your running. Is that accurate, and is there anything else you want me to understand?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's accurate. Being able to run safely is the main thing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Next I'll listen to your lungs, assess your breathing objectively, and watch you use the inhaler. Then we'll agree on an anti-inflammatory treatment and written action plan, including what to do if symptoms worsen or the reliever stops working.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Good. I'd feel better having a clear plan.

flow: Invite the patient's description
Define the exercise pattern and triggers
Measure daytime, nighttime, and activity symptoms
Check severe-attack history
Review reliever response and inhaler technique
Assess smoking, vaping, exposures, and atopy
Explore safety concerns and goals
Summarize and move to objective assessment and an action plan
do_not_miss: Night waking, resting symptoms, and activity limitation
Inability to speak, rapidly worsening breathlessness, or poor reliever response
Previous emergency visits, hospitalization, intensive care, or intubation
Reliever frequency, controller treatment, adherence, and inhaler technique
Smoking, vaping, occupational exposure, and the patient's exercise-safety concern

sources.title: Global Initiative for Asthma ??2026 Strategy Report

pages.h1: Thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss: a model history
pages.meta_description: Read a focused English history for new severe thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss, including urgent screening for a hyperglycemic crisis and the patient's treatment concerns.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Choi, 19, has developed severe thirst, hourly urination, fatigue, and an 8-kilogram unplanned weight loss over three weeks.

voice.direction: A same-day endocrine assessment in clear, efficient American English. The doctor is reassuring but appropriately urgent and checks crisis symptoms early. The patient is a tired 19-year-old man who is worried about diabetes and injections, speaking naturally and clearly.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The rapid progression, extreme thirst, and hourly urination are quantified. Which catabolic symptom should you quantify next?
Weight loss and increased appetite are present, without vomiting, abdominal pain, or abnormal breathing. Which remaining crisis sign should you assess next?
Mental status, infection symptoms, prior glucose history, and family history are clear. Which medicine exposure could change the differential?

recall.cue: The patient is hungry despite rapid weight loss. Ask one direct question that screens for an acute hyperglycemic crisis.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Choi, I'm Dr. Kim. You look tired, so while we check your vital signs, tell me what has changed.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: For about three weeks I've been incredibly thirsty, going to the bathroom all the time, and losing weight even though I'm always hungry.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How quickly have those symptoms been progressing?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: They've become much worse over the last week. I feel drained and weak now.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: About how much are you drinking in a day?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Five or six liters of water. My mouth still feels dry.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How often are you urinating during the day and overnight?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About every hour, and I wake up four or five times a night.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How much weight have you lost?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Eight kilograms in three weeks. I wasn't trying to lose any.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What has happened to your appetite?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's huge. I eat full meals and feel hungry again soon afterward.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you had nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Has your breathing become unusually deep or fast?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, my breathing feels normal.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you felt confused, unusually drowsy, or close to fainting?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I'm exhausted, but I'm thinking clearly and haven't fainted.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Any recent fever, infection, or blurred vision?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No fever or infection. My vision gets a little blurry when I'm very tired.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a high blood sugar reading or another major health problem?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I've always been healthy.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Does diabetes run in your family?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My grandfather developed type 2 diabetes when he was older. No one else that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you take any prescription medicine, over-the-counter product, supplement, or steroid?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, nothing.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: None that I know of.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How is this affecting college, and what worries you most about what might be happening?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I can't stay awake in class, and I keep leaving lectures to urinate. I'm worried it's diabetes, and I'm scared that would mean injections every day.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Let me check that I have this right. Over three weeks you have developed severe thirst, hourly urination including four or five times overnight, increased hunger, fatigue, and an unplanned 8-kilogram weight loss. The symptoms are worsening, but you currently report no vomiting, abdominal pain, unusual breathing, confusion, or fainting. Is that correct, and is there anything else you want to add?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's correct. I mainly want the tests done and to know what happens next.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: These symptoms need prompt assessment today. We'll check your blood sugar and ketones now and do further blood and urine tests as indicated. If you become confused, start vomiting, develop abdominal pain, or breathe deeply and rapidly, we will escalate care immediately. Once we have the results, we'll explain them and discuss any treatment with you rather than assuming what you will need.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Thank you. That helps with the fear.

flow: Assess current appearance while inviting the story
Establish the rapid time course
Quantify fluid intake, urination, and weight loss
Screen immediately for ketoacidosis and dehydration
Check related symptoms and relevant background
Review medicines and steroid exposure
Explore functional impact and fear of injections
Summarize and move to same-day testing
do_not_miss: Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, confusion, drowsiness, or fainting
Degree and speed of weight loss and dehydration symptoms
Recent infection and medications such as glucocorticoids
Family history and prior high glucose readings
The patient's fear of injections without presuming a diagnosis or treatment

sources.title: ADA-led International Consensus ??Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes

pages.h1: A twisted ankle: a model orthopedic history
pages.meta_description: Read a focused English sports-injury history covering ankle injury mechanism, weight-bearing ability, pain location, neurovascular warning signs, prior injury, and return-to-sport goals.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Jin, 28, has right lateral ankle pain, swelling, and bruising after landing awkwardly during basketball four hours ago.

voice.direction: A focused acute musculoskeletal visit in natural American English. The doctor is concise and systematic about mechanism, weight bearing, and neurovascular safety. The patient is a 28-year-old man in moderate ankle pain who is mainly concerned about fracture and returning to basketball.

prediction_pauses.prompt: The inversion mechanism, rapid swelling, and exact pain location are clear. Which weight-bearing question should come next?
He cannot take four steps, but sensation, color, and temperature are normal. Which injury-severity feature should you assess next?
Open injury, deformity, prior sprain, self-care, and pain behavior are established. Which background or recovery goal belongs next?

recall.cue: He could not take four steps immediately after injury. Ask the separate present-time weight-bearing question.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Jin, I'm Dr. Parker. Keep the ankle supported while we talk. Walk me through exactly how you injured it.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: About four hours ago I came down from a rebound in basketball. My right foot rolled inward, and I fell.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did you feel or hear a pop or crack when it happened?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No crack. I felt a sharp pull on the outside of the ankle.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How quickly did the swelling and bruising appear?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It swelled within minutes. The bruising became obvious over the next couple of hours.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Please point with one finger to where it hurts most.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Right over this outer ankle bone and just below it.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Were you able to take four steps immediately afterward?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I managed two steps, then my teammates helped me off the court.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Can you take four steps now, even with a limp?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Putting my full weight on it is too painful.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you noticed any numbness or tingling in the foot?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Has the foot felt cold or looked unusually pale or blue?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. The color and temperature seem normal.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Was there any open wound or an obvious change in the shape of the ankle?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No open cut and no obvious deformity, just swelling.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you injured this ankle before?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I had a mild sprain about three years ago, but it healed completely.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What have you done for it since the injury?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I stopped playing, put ice on it, and kept it raised. I haven't taken pain medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How painful is it while supported, and what makes the pain worse?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: It's about four out of ten while I keep it still, but it becomes sharp and much worse if I move the ankle or try to stand.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any major medical condition or take any regular medicine?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No medical problems and no regular medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have any medication allergies?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No known medication allergies.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What activities are most important for you to get back to?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I sit at a computer for work, but basketball is what I'm worried about. I want to know whether it's broken and when I can play again.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You rolled the right foot inward four hours ago and developed rapid swelling, bruising, and pain over the outer ankle. You could not take four steps then and still cannot now, but you report no wound, deformity, numbness, or change in foot color or temperature. Is that accurate, and is there anything else I missed?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's all correct.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I'll examine the bones, ligaments, movement, circulation, and sensation. Because you cannot take four steps and have pain near the ankle bone, an X-ray may be appropriate after the examination. We'll protect the ankle now and base return to basketball on the findings and your recovery, not on a fixed date.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Okay. I appreciate the clear answer.

flow: Reconstruct the landing and direction of force
Establish immediate swelling and pain location
Ask separately about four-step weight bearing
Screen for open injury, deformity, and neurovascular change
Review prior injury and self-care
Identify work and sport goals
Summarize before examination and imaging decision
do_not_miss: Exact mechanism and direction of the twist
Ability to take four steps immediately and during assessment
Point pain over the malleoli and other Ottawa-rule locations during examination
Open wound, deformity, severe pain out of proportion, numbness, or a cold or discolored foot
Prior injury and the patient's functional and return-to-sport goals

sources.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria ??Acute Trauma to the Ankle

pages.h1: A head injury during basketball: a focused emergency history
pages.meta_description: Read a concise English emergency history after a sports-related head injury, prioritizing mechanism, consciousness, memory, neurologic danger signs, bleeding risk, observation, and safe return to play.
pages.patient_card: Mr. Yoon, 20, has headache, dizziness, and mild nausea four hours after a collision during basketball.

voice.direction: A concise emergency department history in clear American English. The doctor is calm, safety-focused, and keeps checking the patient's alertness without sounding alarmist. The patient is a 20-year-old man with mild headache and dizziness who is anxious about brain bleeding and return to sport.

prediction_pauses.prompt: Mechanism, consciousness, memory, and symptom trajectory are established. Which neurologic danger sign should you ask about next?
There is no vomiting, seizure, focal neurologic change, increasing drowsiness, or neck pain. Which bleeding-risk modifier should come next?

recall.cue: After brief confusion without loss of memory, ask one question about how the current symptoms have changed over time.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Mr. Yoon, I'm Dr. Adams. We'll keep checking your alertness while we talk. Tell me exactly what happened four hours ago.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Another player and I collided during basketball, and his shoulder hit the side of my head. I fell down and felt dazed.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Did you lose consciousness at any point?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I never blacked out.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: What do you remember from just before and just after the hit?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: I remember the play and sitting on the court afterward. My teammate said I seemed confused for about a minute, but I don't have a gap in my memory.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: How have the headache, dizziness, and nausea changed since then?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: The headache is still mild, about four out of ten, and hasn't been getting worse. I'm a little dizzy and nauseated.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you vomited or had a seizure?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Since the hit, have you noticed any new problem with vision, speech, strength, feeling, or walking?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Bright light bothers me a little, but I can see, speak, move, and walk normally.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you become more confused or unusually drowsy, or been difficult to wake?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. I've stayed awake and feel clearer than I did right after the collision.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Do you have pain or tenderness in your neck?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No neck pain.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: I ask because these can change the bleeding risk: do you take a blood thinner, have a bleeding disorder, or use alcohol or drugs before the injury?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No to all of those. I don't take any regular medicine.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: Have you ever had a concussion or another significant head injury?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No, this is the first time.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: If you go home, who could stay with you and watch for a change?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My roommate can stay with me tonight. I'm worried about a brain bleed and wonder if I need a scan. I also want to know when I can practice again.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: You were struck on the side of the head four hours ago and were briefly confused but did not lose consciousness or lose memory. Your mild headache, dizziness, and nausea are not worsening, and you report no repeated vomiting, seizure, new neurologic problem, increasing drowsiness, neck pain, or bleeding risk. Is that correct, and is there anything else I should know?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: That's correct. Nothing else.

turns.speaker: Doctor
turns.text: We'll complete a neurologic and neck examination and use the full findings to decide whether imaging is needed. You must not return to play today. If you go home, your roommate will receive clear written danger signs such as a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, weakness, seizure, or trouble waking you. We'll also give you instructions for classes, driving, follow-up, and a gradual return to sport only after medical clearance.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Understood. I won't go back to practice until I'm cleared.

flow: Confirm current alertness while taking the history
Reconstruct mechanism and timing
Check loss of consciousness and memory
Track symptom severity and direction of change
Screen for neurologic and cervical-spine danger signs
Assess bleeding risk, substances, and prior concussion
Confirm safe observation and patient concerns
Summarize, prohibit same-day return, and give a concrete safety net
do_not_miss: Loss of consciousness, amnesia, confusion, and change in alertness
Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, focal neurologic change, or unequal pupils
Neck pain or tenderness
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, bleeding disorder, and alcohol or drug use
A responsible observer, written return precautions, and no same-day return to play

CDC HEADS UP ??Responding to a Sports-related Concussion
